newsitem.title: USA: GCA stock drawdown seen bullish for coffee futures.
newsitem.headline: GCA stock drawdown seen bullish for coffee futures.

text.p: New York coffee futures are likely to get a boost from monthly inventory data released late Friday showing a sharp drawdown in U.S. coffee stocks, traders and analysts said.

Supplies of green coffee housed in U.S. warehouses fell in October by 351,000 60-kg bags, to 1,260,000 bags, their lowest level since the Green Coffee Association of New York began tracking inventories in January 1980.
"I think it is extremely bullish," said Victor Henriquez, president, Hencorp Becstone in Miami. "The supply situation, with no build up in inventories, is going to keep the market explosive."
The Port of New Orleans posted the largest decline, with stocks falling by 160,000 bags to 521,000 bags, the GCA said. Inventories dropped by 52,000 bags to 86,000 bags in Miami.
Warehouse stocks in Laredo also declined, falling 77,000 bags to 87,000 bags. In New York, inventories decreased by 47,000 bags in the month, to 168,000 bags.
The decline exceeded the expectations of traders, who called for a drop between 200,000 and 300,000 bags in October.
"There has been a lot of talk about a drawdown, but having it down as much as it was, the market will react positively," said Merrill Lynch analyst Judith Ganes.
But some analysts said gains racked up over the past two days were in anticipation of the decline, which may already be at least partially factored into values.
"It is a supportive report, but it may be priced into the market," said Dean Witter analyst Steve Platt. "I do not know if the rally can be sustained. I'm somewhat skeptical."
Low coffee inventories have buoyed the CSCE futures market, where prices settled last week to their highest levels since last March.

The tight supply situation resulted in part from a late harvest in Central America, where heavy rainfall took its toll on coffee-related infrastructure. A truckers' strike in Colombia last month also delayed deliveries of the 1996/97 crop to key consuming countries.

Although the flow of new-crop coffee exports from Latin American producers has begun to increase, industry sources said exports have bypassed warehouses as U.S. processors quickly snapped up the much-needed beans.
But some analysts said the stockpiles are inevitably going to build.
"There is coffee out there and coffee coming in," said Smith Barney analyst Walter Spilka. "You can take (the drawdown) positively, but how long it lasts is the question."

Earlier in the week, the CSCE reported U.S. certified coffee stocks fell by 471 60-kg bags in the week ended Nov. 8 to 333 bags -- or less than two lots of coffee, the lowest level since the exchange started tracking inventories in 1980.

The spot CSCE December contract, which enters a month-long notice period on November 19, still had a relatively high open interest at 4,461 lots as of Thursday -- the equivalent of more than one million bags of coffee.
The CSCE will release its next certified stock report after the close of business on Monday.
